concepts.name: Requirements before components in a system design

questions.prompt: Your peer opens the mock with "Design a support agent for our SaaS product." What does the System Design Primer say to do first?

choices.text: Choose the vector database and the model first, and justify both choices
Scope use cases and constraints: who uses it, how, how many requests per second
Draw the full diagram with caches, queues and load balancers, then refine it as you go
Estimate the monthly bill first, using the largest model's price per token

questions.explanation: The primer's step 1 is to gather requirements and scope the problem: who will use it, how, how many users, what the inputs and outputs are, how much data, how many requests per second, and the read-to-write ratio. The high-level design is step 2, core components step 3, and scaling step 4. Picking a database first commits you before you know the load, which is a common piece of mock feedback.

sources.title: GitHub - donnemartin/system-design-primer: Learn how to design large-scale systems. Prep for the system design interview. Includes Anki flashcards.
sources.claim: The primer's step 1 is to gather requirements and scope the problem: who uses it, how, how many users, inputs and outputs, data volume, requests per second and read-to-write ratio.

questions.prompt: Your peer's written feedback says: "Jumped into components too fast." Describe how you would structure your next 45-minute LLM system design mock.

model_answer.summary: Follow the four steps: scope the requirements, sketch a high-level design, go deep on the core components, then scale it. Put numbers on the requirements before drawing anything.
key_points: Step 1: clarify use cases, constraints and assumptions (users, requests per second, data size, read-to-write ratio)
Estimate the load and token cost from those numbers before choosing components
Step 2: a high-level design with the main components and their connections, each one justified
Step 3: go deep on the core components, such as the data model, the API and the retrieval path
Step 4: find the bottlenecks and scale them (caching, load balancing, horizontal scaling, sharding)

questions.explanation: The System Design Primer's four steps give the interviewer a clear path to follow and stop you designing for requirements nobody asked for. In an LLM design the numbers from step 1 drive the model choice and the cost, so they have to come first.

sources.title: GitHub - donnemartin/system-design-primer: Learn how to design large-scale systems. Prep for the system design interview. Includes Anki flashcards.
sources.claim: The primer's four steps are outline use cases, constraints and assumptions; create a high-level design; design core components; and scale the design by addressing bottlenecks with load balancing, horizontal scaling, caching and sharding.

questions.prompt: Estimate the daily model cost: 10,000 conversations a day, 4 model calls per conversation, 3,000 input and 300 output tokens per call. Assume $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens.

choices.text: $540 a day
$135 a day
$396 a day
$5,400 a day

questions.explanation: Calls per day: 10,000 × 4 = 40,000. Input: 40,000 × 3,000 = 120M tokens × $3/M = $360. Output: 40,000 × 300 = 12M tokens × $15/M = $180. Total $540. $135 forgets the 4 calls per conversation, and $396 prices output tokens at the input rate. Always multiply by calls per conversation: agents make several model calls per user message.

sources.title: Building A Generative AI Platform | Chip Huyen
sources.claim: Huyen says the cost-related metrics to track are the number of queries and the volume of input and output tokens, which is the basis of the per-call token cost estimate (40,000 calls: $360 input + $180 output = $540).

questions.prompt: Same system: 2,500 of the 3,000 input tokens per call are a fixed system prompt and tool definitions, and they are served from the prompt cache. Assume cache reads cost 0.1× the $3/M input price, and ignore cache writes. What is the new daily input cost?

choices.text: $36 a day
$60 a day
$324 a day
$90 a day

questions.explanation: Across 40,000 calls: cached tokens 40,000 × 2,500 = 100M × $0.30/M = $30, and uncached tokens 40,000 × 500 = 20M × $3/M = $60. Total $90, down from $360. $36 prices every input token as a cache read, $60 forgets the cached tokens still cost something, and $324 takes 10% off the whole bill. The 0.1× read price is Anthropic's usual rate as of September 2026; some models differ, and cache writes cost extra.

sources.title: Prompt caching - Claude Platform Docs
sources.claim: Anthropic's pricing table gives cache reads at 0.1x the base input price for most models (with lower multipliers for some newer models) and cache writes at extra cost, so 100M cached tokens cost $30 and 20M uncached cost $60.

sources.title: Building A Generative AI Platform | Chip Huyen
sources.claim: Huyen describes the prompt cache as reusing overlapping prompt segments such as a system prompt across requests.

questions.prompt: Why are output guardrails harder to apply when you stream the response to the user?

choices.text: Streaming responses don't report token usage, so the guardrails have nothing to run on
Guardrails can only inspect the input prompt, never the text the model generates
Partial output is hard to judge, so unsafe text may reach the user before it's blocked
Streaming turns off the model's own safety training for the rest of the response

questions.explanation: Chip Huyen notes that it's hard to evaluate partial responses, so unsafe responses might be streamed to users before the guardrails can decide to block them. That is the trade-off: streaming improves perceived latency, and waiting for the full response lets you check it. Output guardrails exist exactly to inspect what the model generated.

sources.title: Building A Generative AI Platform | Chip Huyen
sources.claim: Huyen notes it is hard to evaluate partial responses, so unsafe responses might be streamed to users before guardrails can decide to block them.

questions.prompt: In Chip Huyen's generative AI platform, which risk is an input guardrail meant to catch?

choices.text: Malformatted JSON in the model's final response
An empty or truncated response from the model
A hallucinated fact or citation in the answer
Private data leaking to an external model API

questions.explanation: Input guardrails protect against leaking private information to external APIs and against jailbreak attempts. They act before the model sees the prompt. Malformatted output, empty responses and hallucinations are failures of what the model produced, so output guardrails catch them.

sources.title: Building A Generative AI Platform | Chip Huyen
sources.claim: Huyen lists leaking private information to external APIs and model jailbreaking as the risks input guardrails address; empty, malformatted and hallucinated outputs are output-guardrail failures.

questions.prompt: Which cache carries the most risk of returning a wrong answer to the user, and why?

choices.text: The prompt cache, because it stores whole answers that can go stale over time
The semantic cache: a bad similarity match returns a different question's answer
The exact cache, because it needs an embedding model call for every single lookup
The exact cache, because hashing the query throws away its meaning and wording

questions.explanation: A semantic cache embeds each query and reuses a cached answer when a past query is similar enough, above a threshold you set. It depends on good embeddings, working vector search and a trustworthy similarity metric, so any of them can fail and serve the wrong answer. A prompt cache reuses processing of a shared prefix, not answers. An exact cache needs no embeddings.

sources.title: Building A Generative AI Platform | Chip Huyen
sources.claim: Huyen says a semantic cache returns cached results when a query's embedding similarity exceeds a threshold, relies on good embeddings, vector search and a trustworthy similarity metric, and can return a wrong answer on a false match.

questions.prompt: Compare prompt caching, an exact response cache and a semantic cache for a support agent. Which would you add first, and what would you check before adding a semantic cache?

model_answer.summary: A prompt cache reuses a shared prompt prefix and can't change the answer, so add it first. An exact cache replays answers to identical queries. A semantic cache replays answers to similar queries, and is worth it only if you measure a high hit rate with acceptable errors.
key_points: A prompt cache reuses the processing of an overlapping prefix (system prompt, tools), cutting input cost and latency without changing the answer
An exact cache returns a stored response only when the query is identical
A semantic cache matches queries by embedding similarity above a threshold, so a bad match returns a wrong answer
Before adding a semantic cache, measure its hit rate and its wrong-match rate on real traffic; it pays off only if the hit rate is high

questions.explanation: Chip Huyen calls the semantic cache's value more dubious than other caching, because many of its parts can fail, and says to evaluate its efficiency, cost and performance risks first. The order follows risk: the prompt cache is safe, and the semantic cache is the only one that can answer the wrong question.

sources.title: Building A Generative AI Platform | Chip Huyen
sources.claim: Huyen distinguishes prompt, exact and semantic caches, calls the semantic cache's value more dubious, says it may be worth it if the hit rate is high, and advises evaluating its efficiency, cost and performance risks first.

sources.claim: Anthropic's docs say prompt caching reuses an identical prompt prefix such as tools and system instructions, reducing processing cost and time.

questions.prompt: Users say the reply "takes forever to start", but once text appears it streams quickly. Which metric should you look at first?

choices.text: Time to first token (TTFT)
Time per output token (TPOT)
Total latency
Output tokens per request

questions.explanation: TTFT is the time until the first token is generated, which is exactly the wait before anything appears. TPOT is the time per output token, which users experience as streaming speed, and they say that part is fast. In an LLM app a long TTFT often comes from work before generation: retrieval, reranking, input guardrails and a long prompt.

sources.title: Building A Generative AI Platform | Chip Huyen
sources.claim: Huyen defines TTFT as the time it takes for the first token to be generated and TPOT as the time to generate each output token.

questions.prompt: Define TTFT, TPOT and total latency. Then estimate the total latency of a 400-token answer with a TTFT of 0.8 s and a TPOT of 20 ms.

model_answer.summary: TTFT is the wait for the first token, TPOT is the time for each later token, and total latency is the time for the whole response. Total ≈ 0.8 s + 400 × 0.02 s ≈ 8.8 s.
key_points: TTFT (time to first token) is the time until the first token is generated
TPOT (time per output token) is the time taken to generate each output token
Total latency is the time to complete the whole response, roughly TTFT + TPOT × number of output tokens
For 400 tokens: 0.8 + 400 × 0.020 = 8.8 s (8.78 s if the first token is counted inside TTFT)

questions.explanation: Chip Huyen's article defines these metrics. The worked estimate shows why long outputs dominate total latency: here 8 of the 8.8 seconds are generation. Cutting output length helps total latency more than shaving TTFT, and streaming hides the wait from the user without shortening it.

sources.title: Building A Generative AI Platform | Chip Huyen
sources.claim: Huyen defines TTFT (time to first token), TPOT (time per output token) and total latency (time to complete the response); 0.8 s + 400 x 0.02 s gives about 8.8 s.

questions.prompt: Which actions structure a requirements-driven LLM system-design mock? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Clarify users, traffic, data size and functional needs first.
Sketch and justify the high-level components before deep details.
Choose sharding before identifying any load or storage constraints.
Estimate model spending without considering input or output token usage.
Investigate core components and address identified scaling bottlenecks.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: the primer begins with use cases, constraints and assumptions. B: Correct: a high-level design establishes the main connections. C: Incorrect: scaling choices should follow requirements and bottlenecks. D: Incorrect: model cost depends on query volume and token usage. E: Correct: detailed component design and scaling are subsequent steps.

questions.prompt: Which statements distinguish prompt, exact and semantic caches? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A semantic cache requires byte-identical queries to return a cached answer.
A prompt cache reuses an unchanged prefix processing result.
An exact response cache reuses results for matching request keys.
A semantic cache can return a wrong answer after an incorrect similarity match.
Prompt caching skips output generation and always returns an old answer.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect: semantic caching permits similar queries above a matching threshold. B: Correct: repeated tools or system content can be processed once and reused. C: Correct: exact matching identifies the same cached item. D: Correct: similarity thresholds and embeddings can produce false matches. E: Incorrect: prompt caching still generates the response output.

questions.prompt: Assuming total latency is TTFT plus TPOT times output count, which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: TTFT measures the delay before the first generated token.
TPOT measures the entire response duration regardless of its token count.
TPOT measures the time taken to generate an output token.
At 0.8 s TTFT and 20 ms TPOT, 400 tokens take about 0.82 s.
At 0.8 s TTFT and 20 ms TPOT, 400 tokens take about 8.8 s.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: TTFT is time to first token. B: Incorrect: TPOT is a per-token measure, not total duration. C: Correct: it describes output generation speed in time per token. D: Incorrect: 400 times 0.020 seconds adds 8 seconds, not 0.02 seconds. E: Correct: under the stated approximation, 0.8 plus 8 equals 8.8 seconds.
